PHI TO ENTERTAIN
THE
Phi Chapter is honored to host the
114th Annual Convention of Psi Upsi
lon. Particularly is this so for it makes the
perfect setting for a celebration of its
90th year of continuous existence on the
campus of the University of Michigan.
Four times previously has the Phi been
so honored. In 1868, 1880, 1896, 1926,
the Annals relates of distinguished edu
cators of the times and loyal brothers,
whose names are still of memory. Tributes
are included as to both program and
entertainment.
With this history in mind we are dedi
cated to making the 1956 Convention and
the Phi 90th Anniversary a memorable
event.
The Committee extends a cordial invi
tation to all our Psi Upsilon brothers to
join us on this occasion.
Our dates of September 5, 6, 7, come
one week prior to the opening of the
School year at the University of Michigan.
As a result we have available very ade
quate housing for both delegates, active
member guests, and alumni guests.
The Chapter house, after 30 years the
outstanding fraternity house on the cam
pus, will be the focal point of the conven
tion and the 90th Anniversary of the Phi.
Delegates will be housed in the Chap
ter house and in Strauss House within one
block of the Chapter house. Stiauss House
is a
part of the East Quadrangle Univer
sity Dormitory and provides sleeping ac
commodations for 100 men. The Chapter
house will quarter 30 men. In addition,
reservations will be available at the Michi
gan Union providing sufficient advance
notice can be had. However, it is under
stood that all undergraduates attending
will be housed in the Phi Chapter House
or Strauss House.
The Phi Alumni Corporation of Psi
Upsilon and the Active Chapter are co
operating to make this an
outstanding
event.
The Alumni Committee appointed by
Brother Donald A. Finkbeiner, '17, Presi
dent of the Phi Alumni Corporation is
composed of WilHam McPherson IV,
Chairman, Wallace D. Riley, '49, Harold

L. C. Jackson, Jr., '34, and Paul W.
Bruske, '26.

Ann Arbor is easily accessible by train,

We are

became a
part of the Campus scene, it has
grown enormously. On our
Campus "the
Diagonal" stiU is the busy thoroughfare
for students, but we have many new build
ings which provide the best facihties for
learning and a
distinguished faculty to
teach therein.
We are anxious to show you our Law
School, our Medical Center, our new
North Campus, where the Phoenix Me
morial for atom research is rising. Our
Business Administration School is housed
in a new building. Our Engineering Col
lege is expanding under Dean George G.
Brown, Delta 17.
Our active Chapter under the leader
ship of Brothers Calvin, Leedy, Olsen,
Spence, Ingwerson, Petrella, and Huston
are filling committee assignments. You will
find them and their committeemen at your
service throughout the Convention.

A VISIT TO THE NEW HOME OF THE NU
By Edward C. Peattie, Phi '06, Editor of The Diamond
D,-. David A. Keys, Nu '15
JUST
a
year ago, the Nu Chapter moved
to its new home when 65 St. George
Street was taken over
by the University of
Toronto.
Before making the purchase, members
of the Building Committee searched the
district for many months, carefully look
ing over
every available property. The
field was limited by property restrictions
and danger of further expropriation by
the University in the not too distant fu
ture. Just when it looked as
though noth
ing suitable could be found, 221 St.
George Street came on the market. It is
ideally suited to a
fraternity with large
downstairs rooms and sleeping accommo
dations for twenty-nine.
The new home of the Nu is
doing a
great deal for the undergraduate Chap
ter. "65" had been allowed to run down,
since it was
only a matter of time when
the University was to take it over. But this
year, in the new home, the Chapter is one
of the strongest in Psi U's history and the
outlook is very bright for this to con
tinue.
In order to have a Chapter House en
tirely free from debt and in good physical
condition, a diive is being launched to
collect $50,000.
On Saturday evening, March 3rd, a
dinner was served as a curtain raiser to
this drive. Fortunately the Chapter dining
room was so
large that it was adequate
for the 130 members who attended.
After toasts to the Queen, the Uni
versity and the Fraternity, a talk on the
history of the Nu from its early struggles
was
given by E. C. Peattie, Phi '06, who
presented the petition of the Chi Delta
Psi Society of the University of Toronto
to the Convention held with the Mu in
1919, where it was voted on
favorably.
The principal speaker of the evening
was brother David A. Keys, Nu '15, Sci
entific Adviser to the President, Atomic
Energy of Canada Limited, who spoke on
the Progress in Atomic Energy from a
Peace point of view.

J. J. EVANS HESSEY, NU '13. DIES
By R. K. Northey, Nu '12
ON MONDAY, March 26, J. J. Evans
Hessey, Nu '13, after a brief illness,
died at St. Lukes Hospital, New York,
at the age of 63.
Evans was born in Chicago but his
early days were
spent in OrilHa, Ontario,
where he attended preparatory schools
and in the Fall of 1909 entered the class
of 1913 at
University College, University
of Toronto. He became a member of Chi
Delta Psi, a local Fraternity, which in
1920 was installed as the Nu Chapter of
Psi Upsilon.
During World War I he served in the
Canadian Officers Training Corps in
Canada and Overseas. Upon being demobiHzed, his business career in pubHshing and advertising commenced with his
appointment as Business Manager of the
European Edition of the Chicago Tribune
in London and Paris from 1919 to 1925.
On his return to America in 1925 he
became Financial
Advertising Manager of
the New York Herald Trwune and in
1934 he joined the staff of This Week
Magazine as
Advertising Manager. In
1948 he became vice-president and Busi
ness
Manager of that organization.
Shortly after becoming estabhshed in
New York he took up again his keen inter
est in the affairs of his Fraternity. In 1938
he was
appointed a member of the Ad
visory Committee of The Diamond and in
1949 became its Chairman. Under his
chairmanship The Diamond took on a
new look, much being done to improve
the contents and format of the magazine
which made it more
Hvely and readable.
The use of photographs on the front cover
of The Diamond, small cuts of the Chap
ter Editors with their communications and
the use of more
pictures generally were
some of the many changes made under his
leadership.
In 1939 he was
appointed a member of
the Board of Governors of the Alumni
Association of Psi Upsilon. He served as
its Secretary from 1942 to 1946 and as
its President from 1946 to 1949. He conJ. J. Evans Hessey, Nu '13
tinned to serve on the Board of Governors
after his retirement as President until
February of this year when he tendered
his resignation because of failing health.
One of the last tasks he undertook for his
Fraternity was as Chairman of the Com
mittee responsible for the New Directory
which is now
pubHshed.

us know that would be Evan's farewell to

LETTERS TO THE EDITORS
It is fine to be presented favorably in a Psi U setting. In varying degrees all Psi U's come to
appreciate the fraternal . bond with choice spirits of their own, of earlier, and of later times.
For most members this means contacts in their own
chapters. You have wisely broadened your
associations. To some extent I have done the same. Without seeing much of him, for instance,
I have felt acquainted with Earl Babst since meeting him at the Dartmouth convention in
1893. And over the years belonging to Psi U has smoothed the way.
Now, as the shadows lengthen, I iind sustenance in fraternal experience when baffled by the
mystery of human existence.
Yours in Psi U.
Edwin O. Smith, Xi '93
January 27, 1956
Due to my extensive wanderings, the November '55 issue of The Diamond has just caught
up with me, and now
perhaps, feeling firmly planted in Syracuse, I can raise my voice in
behalf of Psi Upsilon.
It was
very heartwarming to read about such a
worthy project as the Psi Upsilon Scholarship
Fund which has been initiated by the Psi and Upsilon Alumni. As stated in the article, the
Fund will provide financial assistance for certain undergraduates who might otherwise have
to forego the fellowship of fraternity life or full participation in other college activities. I
enthusiastically endorse this plan, for I can recall vividly the similar problems encountered as
a freshman at the Delta.
The aims and accomplishments of a
fraternity, which we as alumni so well know, are stated
in part in the article as follows :
"He derives a sense of stewardship which makes him a better citizen and a
technique for
'getting along,' which improves his chances to contribute to society."
The daily problems we are confronted with would, indeed, be easier to handle if we
only
knew how to 'get along' with our fellow man.
Fraternity life does help mold the immature
freshman into the mature
graduate who will practice good citizenship and good fellowship.
Brothers Nicholas E. Brown, Upsilon '28, Wilard B. Eddy, Psi '14, and Walter V. Wiard,
Upsilon '22, are to be heartily congratulated for inaugurating so
worthy a
project, I hope, that
will be endorsed by all Psi U's and become a
project of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity.
Yours in the bonds,
John S. Skillman, Delta '46

SECRETARY C
BROTHER
CHARLES SPARKS
THOMAS, Chi '19, is the second mem
ber of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity to serve
as
Secretary of the United States Navy.
In 1885 WilHam ColHns Whitney, Beta
'63, was
appointed Secretary of the Navy
by Grover Cleveland. It will be remem
bered that Chester A. Arthur, Theta 1848,
was President of the United States from
1881 to 1885.
At the outbreak of World War II,
Brother Thomas was called to Washing
ton by the Assistant Secretary of the Navy
for Air, Artemus L. Gates, Beta '18, and
asked to set up the Navy's aircraft pro
curement program.
Charles Sparks Thomas was born in
Independence, Missouri, on
September 28,
1897, the son of Charles Rogers and Delia
Rouse Thomas. His family moved to Los
Angeles, California, in 1911. He attended
the University of California and later
Cornell University. When the United
States entered World War I, he left Cor
nell to become a Naval Aviator.
Between World Wars I and II, Brother
Thomas was active in the merchandising
field. For several years he was
president
and general manager of Foreman and
Clark, a chain of retail stores. He held
directorships in Lockheed Aircraft Corpo
ration, Byron-Jackson Company, Pacific
Finance Corporation, the Broadway-Hale
Department Stores and others. He was
also active in civic and church affairs in
Los Angeles and on the West Coast. He
served as President of the Navy League
in the 11th Region, as
airport commisTHOMAS, CHI '19

sioner for Los Angeles, on the board of
the Good Samaritan Hospital of Los
Angeles, and as vice president of the Los
Angeles Chamber of Commerce.
During World War II, Brother Thomas
estabhshed the Navy's inventory and pur
chasing control program and originated
the Navy Department's first contract ne
gotiation section. He later served as an as
sistant to the then Secretary of the Navy,
James Forrestal.
In recognition of his outstanding war
time services, Brother Thomas received
the Presidential Medal for Merit and the
Distinguished Service Award.
In early 1953, at the request of Presi
dent Eisenhower, he returned to Wash
ington to serve as Under Secretary of the
Navy from February 9 to July 28, 1953.
Because of his background in the logisti
cal field, he was asked by President Eisen
hower to assume the newly created po
sition of Assistant Secretary of Defense
(Supply and Logistics) and served therein
from July 28, 1953 until May 3, 1954.
Brother Thomas became Secretary of

He was married in 1920 to JuHa B.
Hayward of Los Angeles. They have four
children: Hayward Thomas, Epsilon '43,
an officer in the Naval Reserve during
World War II; JuHa Louise, now Mrs.
Frank Alexander of Los Angeles; Charles
Rogers Thomas, a reserve officer in the
Naval Supply Corps, who was on active
duty during the Korean War; and Com
stock Archer Thomas.

versity's chemical engineering course). He is
a
past president of the National Association

man's in 1940, Dean served for twenty years

Society of Safety Engineers from 1924 to
1940.
Karl M. Keefer, Pi '13, is a
special agent
for Excelsior Insurance Co., worked his way

graduating from Syracuse.

Richard Colby Baker

Richard Colby Baker, Theta-Delta '37,
died December 2, 1955, after an illness of
several years' duration.
Brother Baker grew up in Cheshire, Conn.,
where his father operated a
large nursery.
He was initiated into Psi Upsilon in 1934
at the Theta, while studying Electrical En
gineering at Union College, and transferred to
New York University and the Delta in 1935,
taking his degree in Mechanical Engineering
in 1937. After graduation he worked for
the General Electric Company for more than
a
year before going to the Sperry Gyroscope
Co. In January, 1941, he entered flight train
ing with the U. S. Army Air Force and was
on
pre-graduation leave at the time of Pearl
Harbor. He served as maintenance officer in
the Panama Canal Zone until he transferred
ot B-29 training in 1943. He later flew 35
bombing missions out of India with the 20th
Air Force, and 18 Escort Missions out of
Tinian. He was en route to the United States
on
V-J Day, having served all but eight
months overseas. He held 2 DFC's, 4 Air
Medals, and a
special letter of Commenda
tion from General Curtis Le May.
After the war, he was
assigned to USAF
Accident Investigation Group based at Langley Field and the Pentagon. He transferred
to Wright Field for a
year before being
assigned to Upper Air Research at China
Lake, Calif. After two years he was
assigned
to Boeing in Seattle where he played a
major
part in the development and testing of the
air refueling project. He left the service in
1950 and rejoined the General Electric Co.
at its jet engine plant.
Brother Baker married Miss Norma Luders
in 1943 and leaves his wife and four children
who will maintain the family home at 9653
Kenwood Road, Blue Ash, Ohio.

Dr. William A. Spitzley, Phi '95
Dr. WiUiam A. Spitzley, Phi '95, practic
ing surgeon in Detroit and Ann Arbor since
1902, died recently at the age of 82 after a
long illness.
A native of Detroit, Dr. Spitzley received
his medical degree from the University of
Michigan in 1897. He taught surgery at the
University until 1902 and then went into
private practice.
Dr. Spitzley spent three years preceding
World War I studying in Europe and, upon
the outbreak of war, served overseas with the
Harper Hospital Unit, known as Base Hos
pital No. 17.

practice, which continued until his retirement
in 1953. Between 1942 and 1953, in addition

Sanatorium and Harper Hospital; a feUow

president of the Ann Arbor Medical Club
and the Detroit Academy of Medicine.

Dr. Spitzley collaborated with Dr. C. D.
deNancreda, of the University of Michigan,
on the widely used volume, "The Principles
of Surgery."
Brother Spitzley was the possessor of a
superb voice, and his singing, at the 1897
Convention of Psi Upsilon of "Du Bist Wie
Fine Blume," is recorded in the account of
that session in the Annals.
Dr. Spitzley belonged to the University
Club, Detroit Club and the Country Club of
Detroit. His Detroit home was at 1121 Van
Dyke.

nieces and nephews survive.
